title: What game engine has the least friction with AI and fastest workflow?
author: FutureLynx_
selftext:
I asked gpt for the most ai friendly game engine. With less editor friction, and fast workflow. And it told me Godot, as expected. Though i think a Typescript or Phaser workflow could be even better or fast for AI.

Then I asked for something incoming and new that could potentially be even better in this regard and it told me about Hayao, that is a TS, plain code game engine.

I didnt dwelve too much into it, but it looks promissing.

What do you think?

Here it is:

[https://hayao.dev/](https://hayao.dev/)

Though it seems a bit too obscure.

comments.author: TheeJestersCurse

comments.author: Revolutionary-Skin97
comments.body:
Cocos 3.8.X

Its Typscript that compiles into a faster programming language, its also easy to deploy to web or make an app.

so far i think its only limitation is documentation is in CN, but you have AI to identify if a feature you need exist.

Now for its issues, sometimes compilation from TS to its compiled language doesnt translate properly to the point a web can understand it, some examples are .concat or .Array conversions from initial typescript, this can be harnessed easily along the way.

You also would have great support in Cocos since it directly use Spine for animation, just drag and drop the spine file, and its good to go.

comments.author: clockwork_blue
comments.body: I've been using Godot and haven't had a single issue. I've see a lot of people recommending web-based frameworks and engines, but if you want to make anything semi-serious you are gonna have a lot of headaches.

replies.author: FutureLynx_
replies.body: Why? It seems with engines we are fighting the engine sometimes. Full code solutions seem to be more fluid with AI.

replies.author: YKLKTMA
replies.body: Game engines are complex not by choice, but because making a game is a technically difficult task, and the more complex the game is, the more complex the development becomes

replies.author: clockwork_blue
replies.body:
I'm not sure I understand what you mean by "fighting the engine." Are you talking about scene management/placement, having to do things in the engine's canonical way, or just the amount of setup compared to vibecoding something from scratch?

Like, if the goal is to prototype quickly by saying "create some terrain with trees, add a character, let me control it with WASD," then sure, a code-first framework can feel very fluid with AI. But Godot can handle that kind of workflow too.

The difference shows up when you want to take that prototype/demo and turn it into something production-ready. Godot already gives you a mature framework and tooling for things like asset pipelines, scene/resource management, animation, physics, profiling, export, etc. With a web-based framework, sooner or later you're engineering a lot of those solutions yourself.

You also start running into the platform itself: native/C++ code for performance-sensitive systems, real multithreading, networking, and so on. WASM + workers gets you part of the way there, and WebTransport is interesting, but it's still not really equivalent to having a native engine/runtime underneath you.

The one area where I'd give the web stack a pretty clear advantage is UI. AI can generate usable HTML/CSS UI extremely quickly. I wouldn't necessarily say *good* UI. If you don't want it to immediately look like "AI slop," you're still going to want to curate the design yourself. But for a UI-heavy game, that's definitely a plus.

So I can see the argument that a pure-code/web workflow has less friction for the AI. I'm just not convinced that translates into less friction for actually building a serious game.

replies.author: FutureLynx_
replies.body: I meant as you said "just the amount of setup compared to vibecoding something from scratch". Lets say you are using Unreal Engine vs Phaser.js. And we are making a 2D RTS game. Your logic in Unreal will be split into the material editor, the blueprints, the c++ code. And you have post processing, behavior trees. And then you have all the other editor settings. These make things harder to manage than doing it all in a full code solution.

replies.author: clockwork_blue
replies.body: That's why I said Godot, not Unreal Engine.

comments.author: liatris4405
comments.body:
From my experience using both Unity and Godot, I think Godot lets you iterate faster overall. It feels like Godot’s traditional advantage of being lightweight translates directly into a faster development cycle.

Especially with Astra now supporting Computer Use, I’ve found that letting it directly inspect the game on screen and make adjustments seems to improve the accuracy of its changes. In that context, being able to build and launch the game quickly is a real advantage.

On the other hand, Unity and Unreal Engine have much more mature lighting and shading systems. If you simply make use of the features they already provide, it’s relatively easy to get a richer, more polished-looking result. In that respect, I think they have an advantage over Godot.

As for directly working with the GPU pipeline through three.js/WebGL, I haven’t really tried that yet, so I can’t say much about it.

replies.author: FutureLynx_
replies.body: Unreal is a very slow workflow with AI, because of how the engine is tied to blueprints. The whole create C++ class, then create child blueprint is terrible for AI. So i'd say Unity is superior to Unreal in terms of AI workflow. But I worked for years with Unreal Engine only.

replies.author: liatris4405
replies.body: Yeah. Honestly, for the level of graphics most indie games are aiming for, even Unity can feel like overkill. Godot gives you enough control over the basics, including lighting, so I’m currently developing my game in Godot as well.
